frameworks.name: Close Rate Pricing Guide
frameworks.definition: A framework correlating observed close rates to price elasticity, using close rate as a proxy for whether pricing is below market-clearing and how much room for increase exists.

frameworks.name: Tiered Pricing with Decreasing Marginal Rate
frameworks.definition: A pricing structure with fixed base fee and watermarked tiers (e.g., $6k base, +5% above $20k spend, +2.5% above $100k) where higher tiers apply only incrementally, not retroactively.

claims.text: A mid-market service business operating at 25% net margins with $2M revenue at a 60-70% close rate is substantially mispriced. Rory Sutherland's pricing guide indicates a close rate in that range corresponds to at least a 2x price increase, or approximately $6k average monthly retainer, which would increase margins to 50%+, unlocking capital for growth investments.
claims.speaker: Rory Sutherland
claims.mechanism: Higher margins fund growth investments (sales hires, ad spend); low margins create psychological barrier to spending even when ROI is positive. At $6k/month with 50% margins, $250k spend on a new salesperson becomes acceptable.

anchors.region: current state ($2M revenue, 25% margin, 70% close rate)

anchors.value: margins fund growth capital with confidence

claims.text: Businesses at a 60-70% close rate on a flat-fee service offer have likely underpriced precisely because the buyer accepts the price without objection. A buyer's willingness to pay 15k when you quoted that price (and not negotiating down) is a pricing signal—you should have quoted higher.
claims.speaker: Rory Sutherland

claims.text: When a service business transitions to a higher-market avatar (e.g., mid-market instead of SMB), pricing must increase proportionally or the business leaves margin on the table. The agency founder moved upmarket in customer quality but kept pricing constant, creating a margin gap.
claims.speaker: Rory Sutherland

claims.text: The close-rate-to-price-elasticity relationship is structured as follows: 35% close rate indicates correct pricing; 40-50% close rate indicates 25-50% price increase room; 50-60% indicates 1.5x-1.75x increase; 60-70% indicates 2x increase minimum; 70-80% indicates 2-3x increase minimum. Close rate is a market signal of how far below the buyer's willingness-to-pay threshold the quoted price sits.
claims.speaker: Rory Sutherland
conditions: Direct sales model with visible close rate

claims.text: Pricing below the buyer's budget constraint creates a false signal of illegitimacy. A mid-market company considers a $3.5k-$10k service fee suspiciously cheap, inferring that the vendor lacks capability or credibility. Paradoxically, slightly raising price removes the illegitimacy signal and can increase close rates rather than decrease them.
claims.speaker: Rory Sutherland
claims.mechanism: Below-budget pricing triggers buyer skepticism ('if it's this cheap, they can't be good'). Raising price to meet or exceed buyer expectations of service cost restores credibility and can paradoxically improve conversion rate.
bounded_by: Does not apply to price-sensitive SMB segments where absolute price dominates decision
Does not apply to transparent-pricing contexts (SaaS) where low price is an expected feature

claims.text: Founder conviction and limiting beliefs about personal capability are the true constraint on growth acceleration in service businesses, not economics or market conditions. The agency founder can fund growth investments at current margins but psychologically blocks the spending because they internalize a low-price perception, conflating their own low personal income history with what their customers will pay.
claims.speaker: Rory Sutherland
conditions: Founder personal background of modest means
Founder lacks peer group of similarly-or-higher-earning business owners

claims.text: The phrase 'I'm afraid' or 'I'm embarrassed' signals a limiting belief rooted in personal identity or upbringing, not rational business analysis. The agency founder's statement 'I'm embarrassed about winning' and reluctance to raise prices are symptoms of the same underlying belief: 'people won't pay this because I wouldn't pay this,' which is seller's wallet syndrome.
claims.speaker: Rory Sutherland
conditions: Founder exhibits emotional language: fear, embarrassment, shame

claims.text: A service business at $2M revenue operating at 25% net margin generates roughly $400k-$600k SDE (seller's discretionary earnings). Doubling pricing to achieve 50% margins unlocks capital to hire additional salespeople ($250k investment) or increase ad spend without psychological resistance, because the margin cushion makes the spending feel safe.
claims.speaker: Rory Sutherland

anchors.value: $1M SDE; sufficient for $250k+ hiring or ad spend

claims.text: The tiered pricing structure with non-retroactive watermarks (base $6k flat for first $20k ad spend, +5% above $20k, +2.5% above $100k) creates survivorship bias where customers aspire to reach the lowest-cost tier at the top. This tier design eliminates internal conflict about price justification because margin is purely incremental above each threshold.
claims.speaker: Rory Sutherland
conditions: Desire to avoid retroactive repricing friction

claims.text: Churn improvement from 'quite high' to 10-20% annually correlates with upmarket avatar transition. The agency founder's observation that churn decreased after focusing on mid-market clients (not SMBs) suggests that mid-market customers are inherently stickier than SMB customers, and the founder's delivery quality matches mid-market expectations better.
claims.speaker: Rory Sutherland
conditions: Service business transitioning from SMB to mid-market avatar

claims.text: The limiting belief 'I can't spend past X dollars per day on ads' (e.g., '$1,000/day') or 'I don't make enough money per customer' is a founder projection, not a market constraint. The founder conflates their own psychological spending threshold (shaped by childhood scarcity) with the customer's willingness to pay. Both beliefs are barriers to testing.
claims.speaker: Rory Sutherland
conditions: Founder reporting emotional block to scaling spend

examples.text: The agency founder stated they recently closed a 15k-per-month deal without the client 'batting an eye' or negotiating. Rory's interpretation: the client accepted $15k readily, which means $15k was below their budget constraint and the deal was underpriced. This deal serves as proof that mid-market customers have larger budgets and higher price acceptance than the founder's then-pricing reflected.

The agency founder reported moving upmarket to mid-market customers (from SMBs) and simultaneously improving churn from high rates to 10-20% annually with the help of VP Jean-Francois. However, pricing remained at $3.5k-$10k per month. Rory's diagnosis: the avatar moved but pricing didn't follow, leaving margin on the table and creating psychological scarcity that blocks growth investment.

The founder described their personal background as 'pretty modest, pretty poor-ish, suburban poor' and stated they now lack confidence to price higher or spend more on growth investments. Rory reframed this as 'selling out of your own wallet'—analogous to a mechanic refusing to pay for an oil change because they know how to do it themselves. The founder's personal experience of price doesn't match their customers' budgets.

practices.text: Test a price increase by implementing tiered pricing with non-retroactive watermarks: $6k base fee (flat) for ad spend $0-$20k, then +5% for each additional dollar up to $100k, then +2.5% above $100k. The key is that these percentages apply only to the new tier, not retroactively to all spending.

Set a minimum customer spending threshold (e.g., 'must spend at least $20k/month on ads') as a requisite for being a customer. This filters out SMB noise and positions your service for mid-market economics.

When you observe a 60-70% close rate on a service offer, immediately test a price increase (start with +50%) rather than assuming pricing is correct. Use the close rate as a market signal of how far below willingness-to-pay your quote sits.

If emotional language ('I'm afraid,' 'I'm embarrassed') appears when discussing pricing or growth spending, name the limiting belief explicitly rather than proceeding with business logic. The belief is the bottleneck, not the economics.
